title: 01 · Read the indices
prompt: In pi[n,i,j], what does each index identify?
options: n importer, i exporter, j industry.
n exporter, i importer, j industry.
n importer, i industry, j exporter.
explanation: Shares have shape (N,N,J). For each importer/industry, shares sum to one over exporters, axis 1.

title: 02 · Match code to an equation
prompt: Select the block that computes the denominator of the trade-share equation in log space.
explanation: row_logsumexp sums over exporters within each importer/industry. It returns (N,J) log denominators; broadcasting [:,None,:] normalizes the (N,N,J) weights.

title: 03 · Close the economy
prompt: Explain country-level market clearing, the damped wage update, and how normalized Cobb–Douglas utility defines cost of living.
explanation: Country sales sum pi[n,i,j]*alpha[n,j]*income[n] over importers and industries. They equal w[i]L[i]; individual industry trade need not balance. Damping multiplies wages by (sales/income)^0.2 before country-0 normalization. Utility product(c/alpha)^alpha has C=product P^alpha and real wage w/C; expenditure shares remain alpha.
rubric: Equates aggregate exporter sales with country income; distinguishes industry trade from aggregate balance.
Explains q>1/q<1, fixed damping, normalization, and the full residual check.
Derives C=product P^alpha for normalized utility and unchanged spending shares.

title: 04 · Change the numeraire
prompt: If all wages are rescaled by a common positive factor, what happens?
options: Prices scale by the same factor; trade shares and real wages are unchanged.
Prices stay fixed and real wages scale.
Trade shares scale by the same factor.
explanation: Industry prices and aggregate cost of living are homogeneous of degree one in wages. Common nominal scaling cancels from trade shares and w/C. Both verification routes must use the same wage normalization.

title: 05 · Supply exact hats
prompt: Which information enters the exact-hat equilibrium equations for this trade-cost shock?
options: Baseline industry shares and country incomes, theta[j], alpha[n,j], and trade-cost hats.
Only the new trade costs and gamma.
Counterfactual wages from the levels solver.
explanation: Hats reweight baseline shares by wage and trade-cost ratios using industry elasticities. Fixed preferences allocate country spending and aggregate industry price hats. Gamma cancels; the shocked costs are validated using retained primitives.

title: 06 · Explain two routes
prompt: Why should E1/E0 equal exact hats? How does the J=1 regression add evidence, and what does agreement fail to prove?
explanation: Identical primitives except for the shock, fixed preferences, closure and numeraire imply identical ratios. J=1 with alpha=1 compares the generalized code against frozen outputs from accepted PR #4, including C=P. Agreement still requires converged full residuals and does not establish human understanding.
rubric: Explains the same shock, fixed preferences, closure and numeraire across routes.
Explains J=1, alpha=1, C=P and the immutable accepted reference.
Separates numerical consistency from convergence, specification review and learner understanding.

title: 07 · Diagnose a false pass
prompt: All comparison errors are 1e−13 and wage changes are tiny, but the hat route reaches max_iterations with a full residual of 2e−4. What is the verdict?
options: Fail: the hat route has not converged, despite matching outputs.
explanation: Fail: small steps can reflect strong damping or stagnation. The iteration must reach its full residual target (default 1e−13), and verification requires all routes to converge, residual norms below 1e−11, and both error measures below 1e−9. An iteration-limit status is not convergence.

title: 08 · Interpret the shock
prompt: Industry 0's bilateral costs fall 10%, while industry 1's costs stay fixed. Trace the effect on wages, both industries, aggregate prices and country 2's welfare.
explanation: Direct competitiveness changes in industry 0 alter demand and country incomes. Shared wages feed into both industries, so industry 1's shares and prices can respond without its own cost shock. C=product P^alpha weights those prices; welfare is w/C. Country 2 responds through world demand and wage adjustments.
rubric: Identifies the direct industry-0 competitiveness effect and shared-wage spillovers.
Explains fixed alpha, aggregate price changes, and welfare w/C.
Explains why country 2 and the unshocked industry can respond.
